tldr: Using a unified, custom-built hat-mounted sensor device called "RoboCap," this open dataset captures 10,000 hours of unscripted manipulation performed by workers during real paid shifts across 11 countries, providing online-calibrated millimeter- and centimeter-accurate 3D head and bimanual hand trajectories along with language instructions.
hero_caption: Estimated 3D hand meshes (MANO model) across diverse real-world settings worldwide, including fabric cutting, auto maintenance, confectionery making, and PCB soldering. Even with gloves, heavy tool and object grasping, occlusions, and complex lighting conditions, high-precision 3D poses of both hands are robustly captured.
overview:
In training robot foundation models, the scarcity of physical interaction data in the real world is the biggest bottleneck. Because teleoperation is expensive and hard to scale, first-person (egocentric) video captured with human head-mounted cameras has drawn high expectations as a low-cost, scalable source. However, existing datasets have faced major hurdles: monocular cameras leave 3D scale ambiguous, reliance on built-in trackers of commercial headsets prevents re-estimation from raw data, and federating heterogeneous devices introduces uneven quality.

To solve this, the authors designed "RoboCap," a lightweight hat-mounted device equipped with six synchronized wide-angle global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. With it, they recorded 10,000 hours of unscripted bimanual manipulation during real work shifts (in factories, kitchens, farms, workshops, and more) across 11 countries. By strictly unifying the hardware to a single model and applying per-session online calibration to correct minor camera misalignments caused by operational heat and mechanical stress, they kept epipolar errors below 1 pixel. This enables gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories via visual-inertial SLAM and cm-precise 3D bimanual hand poses (MANO) from multi-view tracking across all frames.

Furthermore, the corpus includes sparse descriptions of overall episode goals alongside dense language annotations for temporally segmented sub-tasks. Both the raw data and estimated labels are released in LeRobot and Rerun formats. This serves not only as valuable pre-training data for robot learning, but also as a foundational benchmark to study how action label accuracy impacts policy performance.
contributions: Collected and curated 10,000 hours of real-world occupational manipulation across 11 countries, 18 task families, and 2,000 tasks using a single-model hat device, RoboCap.

Achieved sub-1 px epipolar error via per-session online rotational calibration, providing all frames with gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories in a world frame and cm-precise 3D bimanual hand poses (MANO).
Provided a two-tier language annotation scheme consisting of sparse goal descriptions for entire episodes and dense descriptions of sub-tasks and low-level actions for segmented time intervals.
Fully released the approximately 127 TB dataset under a commercially permissive CC BY 4.0 license, formatted for direct compatibility with the LeRobot learning library and Rerun visualization tool.

sections.heading: Why does robot learning need metrically accurate egocentric video?
sections.summary: Unlike language and vision foundation models, robot learning faces a severe shortage of real-world interaction data. Egocentric video is a promising source, but existing datasets lack metric 3D scale or remain confined to restricted lab environments, missing the geometric accuracy required for real robot control.
sections.details:
The biggest roadblock to general-purpose robots is the data shortage. While robot teleoperation yields high-quality demonstrations, collecting it is prohibitively expensive and cannot cover the long tail of diverse environments. Consequently, human egocentric video has attracted immense interest as a cheap, scalable way to record smooth physical manipulation in the real world.

However, to turn video into supervision for robot actions, one must infer human hand and head movements from the footage. Recent scaling studies demonstrate that pre-training on massive egocentric video improves policy generalization, and unlocking its full benefit demands accurate 3D hand pose labels. Hardware is the critical bottleneck here. Most existing datasets use monocular cameras, where absolute distance can only be guessed. Stereo cameras directly yield metric scale, but they are extremely sensitive to calibration. On RoboCap's geometry, a mere 1-pixel disparity error translates to roughly a 1 cm depth error at a 0.65 m working distance—comparable to the grasp tolerance of typical parallel-jaw grippers.

Additionally, relying on motion-capture labs or VR headset internal trackers restricts capture environments and discards raw multi-view video, preventing researchers from re-estimating poses with better future algorithms. To overcome these limitations, this work introduces "RoboCap-10k," a curated corpus of 10,000 hours of manipulation gathered across real workplaces in 11 countries using a single wearable device design and a unified processing pipeline.

sections.heading: How does RoboCap-10k differ from existing egocentric datasets?
sections.summary: Previous large-scale egocentric datasets were predominantly monocular or centered on domestic chores, struggling with 3D label precision and hardware heterogeneity. RoboCap-10k stands apart with its single calibrated hardware model, per-session self-calibration, and coverage of genuine, unscripted occupational tasks across diverse workplaces.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Large-Scale Egocentric Datasets
Early corpora like Ego4D captured diverse daily activities, but relied heavily on monocular, rolling-shutter cameras unsuited for precision 3D reconstruction. Recent datasets tailored for robotics (such as Egocentric-10K and EgoSuite) remain monocular or federate heterogeneous devices, which introduces unavoidable domain shifts in appearance and 3D metric accuracy. RoboCap-10k uses a single device design featuring two stereo baselines optimized for near-field manipulation and lateral cameras, focusing on real occupational work rather than staged domestic scripts.

### 2.2 Egocentric Visual-Inertial SLAM
Head-mounted SLAM must cope with rapid head turns, extreme near-field parallax, and severe view occlusions caused by the hands. Moreover, wearable hardware deforms under thermal and mechanical stress, causing relative camera rotations to drift by 0.2° to 1.1° (median ~0.5°). This drift produces 1 to 5 px of epipolar residual, inducing a 1 to 2 cm depth bias at arm's length. This work resolves the issue by running per-session rotational self-calibration across the entire dataset.

### 2.3 3D Hand Pose Estimation and Robot Learning
Monocular hand pose estimation relies on weak-perspective assumptions, leaving absolute scale ambiguous. Multi-view fusion can resolve this ambiguity, but has traditionally been confined to MoCap studios. The tracker in this work employs a model trained on multi-view optimization of in-the-wild video. This substantially cuts down the label noise introduced when retargeting human motions into robot joint spaces.

sections.heading: How the RoboCap device and 3D reconstruction pipeline work
sections.summary: A 250 g hat carries six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. Per-session online calibration eliminates rotational drift, while multi-camera VIO SLAM and a multi-view ViT hand tracker recover high-precision head and hand trajectories.
sections.details:
### 3.1 The RoboCap Hat Device
RoboCap uses a 250 g hat design that distributes its weight across the crown of the head, avoiding pressure on the nasal bridge during long work shifts. It carries six global-shutter cameras running at 1920×1080 and 30 Hz. Two stereo pairs (baselines of 86.8 mm and 106.2 mm; FOVs of 157° and 154°) sit at the forehead and eye level, ensuring the entire manipulation workspace is covered in stereo. Two lateral wide-angle cameras face obliquely downward (85° outwards, 30° downwards) so that egomotion tracking continues uninterrupted even when hands occlude the front cameras. All cameras are hardware-synchronized by a single PWM signal and time-synced with two 6-axis IMUs (200 Hz) using an onboard TCXO clock.

### 3.2 Factory and Online Calibration
While high-precision initial factory calibration (Kannala-Brandt distortion model) is performed using an AprilGrid target, field recordings suffer rotational drift from mechanical and thermal stress. To counter this, the rotation component $\mathbf{R}_c \in SO(3)$ of all six cameras is jointly re-estimated for every single recording session. Factory translation baselines are kept fixed to preserve metric scale, while corresponding keypoints across overlapping camera pairs are jointly optimized using a robust Huber loss. This brings the mean Sampson error below 1 px across every device.

### 3.3 Visual-Inertial SLAM and Hand Pose Estimation
Head trajectories are tracked using a sliding-window VIO (GroundedSLAM) across four cameras: the front stereo pair and the two lateral cameras. After each session, an offline bundle adjustment over all keyframes yields gravity-aligned 6-DoF trajectories in world coordinates, roughly doubling the precision of real-time estimation. For hand tracking, a multi-view Vision Transformer takes cropped hand patches from all views where hands appear, outputting geometrically consistent MANO parameters and 21 keypoints (16 joints + 5 fingertips) that align perfectly across cameras.

captions.F2: Hand pose estimation results under challenging operational environments. Even with gloves, stains, and heavy tool contact during bread dough shaping, pharmaceutical sorting, woodworking, and automotive engine teardown, the blue (left) and magenta (right) MANO meshes fit accurately.

sections.heading: Structuring 10,000 hours of authentic work across 11 countries
sections.summary: Ten thousand hours (about 1.38 million episodes) were curated from unscripted shifts of workers in 11 countries. The dataset features a three-tier task taxonomy, two-tier language captions, and comprehensive face anonymization.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Design Philosophy and Collection Protocol
The corpus was built around four core principles: environmental diversity, task diversity with hierarchy, metrically accurate action labels, and standardized hardware. Participants were employees at partner enterprises across 11 countries (including India, the Philippines, Indonesia, Malaysia, Nigeria, and Colombia) who wore the hat during their normal 6- to 12-hour work shifts. There was no scripting or staging. From the raw footage, segments lasting between 10 and 600 seconds (median 17.8 seconds) with clear bimanual interaction and successful SLAM/hand tracking were extracted as "episodes."

### 4.3 Task Taxonomy
Episode descriptions were clustered using a language model into a three-tier taxonomy spanning 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 distinct tasks. Tasks are categorized by difficulty: Easy (single-step, 769 tasks), Medium (multi-step, 761 tasks), and Hard (skilled manipulation, 470 tasks). Industrial machine sewing, crop harvesting, food processing, and manual assembly dominate the top ranks, creating a rich long tail of skilled manual work.

### 4.4 Sparse and Dense Language Captions
To support instruction-following policy training, the dataset provides two levels of language annotations:
- **Tier 1 (Sparse Captions)**: A single sentence describing the overall episode objective (e.g., "tear and fold a paper towel, then wipe the beaker").
- **Tier 2 (Dense Captions)**: Non-overlapping temporal segments detailing sub-tasks. Each segment includes three elements: the workspace "scene", the sub-goal "high_level_task", and the physical motion "low_level_task". These were consistently generated from the front stereo video using Gemini 3.8 Flash.

### 4.5 Formatting and Face Anonymization
The corpus is hosted on Hugging Face in LeRobot v3.0 format (Parquet + MP4, totaling 127 TB) and supports synchronized 3D visualization in Rerun. For privacy protection, a custom face detector trained on fisheye distortion and steep pitch angles was developed, applying tracked and dilated irreversible Gaussian blurring to faces without obscuring the hand workspace.

captions.F4: Data distribution and taxonomy in RoboCap-10k. (a) Proportion of recorded hours and task counts across task families. (b) Cumulative distribution of the 2,000 tasks ranked by recorded hours. While the top 500 tasks account for 53% of the data, a substantial long tail of rare tasks is captured.
captions.F5: Examples of face detection and anonymization on field footage. Even with faces distorted near the edges of fisheye lenses, steep overhead pitch angles, or partial occlusions by tools, faces are accurately detected and blurred while strictly preserving the hand manipulation area.

sections.heading: Millimeter-level verification: How accurate are the labels?
sections.summary: Rigorous evaluations were conducted against external benchmarks and high-precision optical motion capture. Online calibration achieved a median residual error of 0.62 px, SLAM trajectories reached an average error of 3.19 mm, and hand joint position error was within 4.5 mm.
sections.details:
### 5.1 Calibration Accuracy
Evaluating Sampson error on held-out feature matches across all recording sessions, the median per-device error was 0.62 pixels for both the forehead and eye-level stereo pairs. Even the worst-performing device achieved 0.99 pixels, confirming that every single unit met the target threshold of less than 1 pixel.

### 5.2 SLAM Accuracy Evaluation
On the city-scale walking benchmark LaMAria, the SLAM pipeline scored 72.4, closely trailing Aria's official SLAM at 75.9. Furthermore, absolute trajectory error (ATE) was measured on "RoboMoCap," a 153.4-hour optical motion capture dataset (NOKOV, 120 Hz) recorded while wearing RoboCap. On held-out sessions, the median ATE was 3.0 mm (mean 3.19 mm). Scale drift showed a median error of only 0.17%, proving that millimeter-level geometric consistency is preserved in the world coordinate frame.

### 5.3 Hand Pose Estimation Accuracy
Using the RoboMoCap test set (9.2 minutes), Procrustes-aligned mean per-joint position error (PA-MPJPE) was evaluated to isolate structural pose error from individual hand anatomy differences. The pipeline achieved an average error of 4.5 mm across all 21 keypoints. On a synthetic and real benchmark with known hand meshes (GSI-Internal), the absolute joint error (MPJPE) was 9.2 mm, consistently staying below the 1 cm mark.

captions.F6: Held-out Sampson error distributions across all devices after online calibration. Both the forehead stereo (left) and eye-level stereo (right) show a median error of 0.62 px, with all units achieving geometric alignment well below the 1 px threshold (dashed line).

sections.heading: Remaining challenges and caveats for dataset use
sections.summary: Key limitations include fingertip occlusions during tight grasps due to inferred labels, geographic imbalance across countries, the absence of force/tactile feedback, and the embodiment gap between human hands and robot manipulators.
sections.details:
There are four primary limitations to keep in mind when utilizing this dataset:

- **Inferred Labels**: The 3D poses are outputs of an automated reconstruction pipeline rather than direct sensor ground truth. Local errors can occur when contact surfaces between fingertips and grasped objects are completely occluded during heavy power grasps.
- **Geographic and Task Imbalance**: While the dataset covers 11 countries, roughly two-thirds of the data originates from India and the Philippines. Furthermore, because only segments meeting strict bimanual tracking criteria were extracted, unimanual tasks and extreme low-light environments are underrepresented.
- **Lack of Force/Tactile Data**: No contact force or torque measurements are included; contact dynamics must be deduced entirely from visual cues.
- **Embodiment Gap**: The degrees of freedom and appearance of human hands and forearms differ fundamentally from robotic grippers and arms. Successfully transferring these policies to physical robots still requires effective kinematic retargeting and domain adaptation.

sections.heading: A 10,000-hour foundation for the future of robot learning
sections.summary: RoboCap-10k reconciles large-scale collection with rigorous geometric tracking on a single standardized hardware platform. Releasing all raw multi-view video alongside metric labels significantly advances generalization in robot foundation models.
sections.details:
RoboCap-10k harmonizes two goals that were long at odds: the sheer data scale of human first-person video and the metric geometric precision demanded by robot control. This was realized through a dedicated custom wearable device and an automated self-calibration pipeline.

The resulting 10,000 hours of rich physical manipulation from authentic workplaces worldwide offer unmatched pre-training data for general-purpose robot manipulation policies and video world models. Crucially, because all raw, synchronized high-resolution multi-view video is preserved and published, researchers can re-infer the entire label set whenever superior 3D tracking models emerge. It stands as a vital empirical platform to answer a central open question: how much does the geometric accuracy of human action labels matter when scaling robot foundation models?

takeaways: Instead of monocular capture, a multi-view stereo configuration optimized for the manipulation workspace paired with per-session online self-calibration is the key to sub-centimeter 3D hand and head tracking.

Unlike scripted domestic tasks, authentic occupational activities worldwide (factories, agriculture, repair, food prep) offer contact-rich manipulation and a massive long tail critical for robot policy generalization.
Beyond raw video, the release includes 3D trajectories in LeRobot format, two-tier language captions, and synchronized Rerun visualizations, making it immediately ready for policy training.
limitations: Although 3D labels are high-precision estimates, local tracking errors remain inevitable when fingertips are occluded against grasped objects.
About 66% of the 10,000 hours comes from two countries (India and the Philippines), creating geographic and task-type imbalances.
Downstream algorithms must bridge the embodiment gap (differences in appearance and kinematics between human hands and robot end-effectors) and cope with the absence of force and tactile sensing.
